title: Acute Stress Response
subtitle: Rapid survival mobilisation after threat
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating acute stress response across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain acute stress response in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in acute stress response.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to acute stress response.

sections.explainSimply: Acute stress prepares the body to act through fast autonomic and hormonal responses.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Attention narrows, salience rises, memory encoding changes and flexible reasoning may temporarily reduce as survival priorities dominate.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Catecholamines act rapidly; HPA-axis cortisol follows more slowly. Response magnitude depends on predictability, controllability, prior learning and current safety.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of acute stress response as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need acute stress response to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A strong acute response can be adaptive and is not itself a disorder.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use acute stress response to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses acute stress response to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: A strong acute response can be adaptive and is not itself a disorder. Evidence classification: established physiology.
